title: State and Data Layer Design
summary: Splitting UI state from client cache from server cache, normalizing fetched data, choosing a cache-invalidation strategy, and applying optimistic updates safely.

slides.markdown:
Ask five engineers where a large app's state "lives" and you'll get five different answers — because most apps have three genuinely different kinds of state stuffed into one bucket. Untangling them is the single highest-leverage decision in a frontend architecture.

This topic covers the three-layer model — UI state, client cache, server cache — how to normalize fetched data so two components never disagree about the same entity, how to invalidate a cache without either serving stale data or refetching everything, and how to make an update feel instant with optimistic UI. Get this layer wrong and every other part of the app inherits the bugs.

slides.sectionTitle: Three kinds of state, one word
slides.markdown:
"State" is used to mean three genuinely different things, and conflating them is where most state-management pain comes from:

- **UI state** — ephemeral, local, disposable on refresh: is this accordion open, what's typed in a not-yet-submitted field, which tab is active.
- **Client cache** — data that *originated* on the server but is held client-side for reuse: a fetched list of posts, a user's profile, cached so re-visiting a screen doesn't re-fetch instantly.
- **Server state, mirrored** — the client cache is never the source of truth, only a copy; the server can change it independently (another user edits the same post), so the copy can go stale at any moment.

The practical rule: UI state belongs in local component state; client-cache state belongs in a data-fetching library (React Query, SWR, Apollo) built for exactly this, not in a general state container. Putting fetched data in the same global store as UI state is the most common design mistake this topic exists to prevent.

Picture a typical SPA screen as three stacked layers feeding the render. The bottom layer is the **network/server** — the actual source of truth. Above it sits the **client cache** — a local, possibly-stale mirror, keyed by entity ID, populated by fetches and updated by mutations. On top sits **UI state** — ephemeral, per-component, never persisted.

Data flows up: a fetch populates the cache, the cache feeds the component. Writes flow down: a mutation goes to the server and then either refetches or directly patches the cache. UI state never touches the network directly — if a modal's open/closed flag started living in the same store as fetched posts, you'd have no way to reason about which parts of that store need revalidation and which don't.

slides.subTitle: Entities by ID, not nested blobs
slides.markdown:
A naive cache stores API responses as-is: the feed screen's cache entry is a nested array of post objects, each with a full embedded author object. The comments screen's cache entry independently embeds that same author again. Now the same user's display name lives in two places, and editing a profile doesn't update both.

**Normalization** stores each entity once, keyed by ID, in a flat lookup — `posts: {id -> post}`, `users: {id -> user}` — and every reference elsewhere is just an ID pointing into that table. The feed screen's state becomes an *ordered list of post IDs* plus a pointer into the shared `posts`/`users` tables, so updating a user updates every screen that references them, instantly and consistently.

This is the same idea as third normal form in a relational database, applied to client memory instead of disk — and it's why libraries like Apollo and Redux Toolkit's `createEntityAdapter` build normalization in by default rather than leaving every team to reinvent it.

"When does cached data get refetched" has three common answers, and picking the wrong one either serves stale data or hammers the server:

| Strategy | How it works | Best for | Risk |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Time-based (TTL)** | Refetch if cached data is older than N seconds | Data that changes at a predictable rate (a stock price feed) | Stale between the change and the TTL expiry |
| **Event-based** | Refetch when a specific action fires (a mutation, a websocket push) | Data invalidated by known user or server actions | Misses changes from actions the client didn't observe |
| **Tag-based** | Every fetch is tagged with the entities it touched; a mutation invalidates all cache entries sharing that tag | Complex apps with many interdependent views of the same entities | More setup — every query and mutation must be tagged correctly |

Most production apps combine all three: a short TTL as a safety net, event-based invalidation on the mutations you control, and tag-based invalidation (as in RTK Query or Apollo's cache) once enough screens read overlapping data that manual tracking becomes unreliable.

Waiting for a round trip before showing a like count increment feels sluggish, even at 150ms. **Optimistic updates** flip the order: apply the change to the local cache immediately, send the mutation in the background, and only reconcile if the server disagrees.

The pattern has three steps every time: (1) snapshot the current cache value so you can restore it, (2) write the optimistic value into the cache and let the UI re-render instantly, (3) on the response, either confirm (usually a no-op, since you already showed the right state) or roll back to the snapshot and surface an error.

The hard part isn't the happy path — it's step 3's failure branch, and specifically making the rollback feel like a deliberate UI state rather than a flicker, which the next slide covers with real code.

slides.sectionTitle: When optimistic updates are the wrong call
slides.markdown:
Optimistic updates aren't free — they're a bet that the mutation almost always succeeds and that showing the wrong answer briefly is an acceptable cost when it doesn't. That bet doesn't hold everywhere:

- **High-stakes, low-probability-of-success actions** — submitting a payment shouldn't optimistically show "success" before the charge actually clears; showing then reverting a payment confirmation erodes trust far more than a brief spinner would.
- **Actions with server-side validation the client can't replicate** — a username-change that might collide with an existing user can't be optimistically confirmed client-side, because the client doesn't know the answer yet.
- **Irreversible actions** — a delete is a reasonable candidate for optimistic UI (undo it by re-inserting on failure), but a send-email action isn't reversible if the optimistic guess was wrong.

The senior-level framing: optimistic updates trade a small chance of a visible correction for a large perceived-speed win, and that trade is only worth making when the failure case is cheap and honest to show.

slides.sectionTitle: Server-truth conflicts: when the client and server disagree
slides.markdown:
Even without optimistic updates, two clients can each hold a cached copy of the same entity that drifts out of sync — user A cached a post's like count at 40, user B liked it seconds later making it 41, and A's screen still shows 40 until something triggers a refetch.

The practical fixes layer on top of what's already covered: short TTLs bound how stale a read can be; event-based invalidation on the mutations *you* fire fixes your own writes; but *other users'* writes are only caught by either polling, a websocket/SSE push that invalidates the relevant cache tag, or accepting the staleness window as fine for this specific entity (a like count 2 seconds stale is rarely a problem; an inventory count showing an out-of-stock item as available is).

Naming which of these three you'd pick — and why the entity's staleness tolerance decides it — is a stronger answer than assuming any one general solution covers every entity in the app.

slides.sectionTitle: Pitfall: two components disagreeing because the cache wasn't the single source of truth
slides.markdown:
**Wrong pattern:** a feed item component copies `post.likeCount` into local component state on mount so it can update it locally on like/unlike, while the post-detail modal reads the same post directly from the shared cache. Like the post from the feed, and the modal (if opened) still shows the old count.

**Why it happens:** copying server data into local state feels convenient in the moment — no need to thread cache-update logic through — but it silently forks a second, unsynchronized copy of an entity that already has one canonical home.

**Correct model:** every component that renders a server entity reads it from the shared client cache, keyed by that entity's ID, never copies it into local state. If a component needs to show an entity as it's being edited before submit, that draft state is UI state living separately — not a copy of the cached entity — so there's exactly one place the actual `likeCount` lives.

Interviewers rarely expect you to build a cache from scratch, but they do expect you to justify a library choice:

| | React Query / SWR | Redux + RTK Query | Apollo Client |
|---|---|---|---|
| Best fit | REST APIs, want caching without a global store | Already using Redux for UI state too | GraphQL APIs specifically |
| Normalization | Per-query cache, not fully normalized by default | Normalized via entity adapters | Fully normalized by entity `id` automatically |
| Learning curve | Low | Medium — Redux concepts plus RTK Query | Medium-high, GraphQL-specific |

The interview-safe framing: pick based on the API shape (REST vs GraphQL) and whether the app already has a global store for other reasons — don't default to Redux for server-cache duties just because it's familiar; that's exactly the layer-conflation this topic opened with.

A senior answer to any "design the data layer for X" prompt names all four decisions in this topic explicitly, in order: which pieces are UI state versus client cache; how the entities involved are normalized so one update reflects everywhere at once; which invalidation strategy fits each entity's staleness tolerance; and where optimistic updates are worth the risk versus where a slower, honest confirmation is the safer call.

Getting this right up front is what prevents the two most common production bugs in large SPAs: components silently showing different values for the same entity, and a cache that either serves stale data for minutes or refetches so aggressively it saturates the API.
